templates.pattern: An atom has [P] protons and [N] neutrons in its nucleus. Calculate the mass number of the atom.
templates.explanation:
Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons
= [P] + [N]
= [RESULT]

The mass number is the total number of nucleons (protons and neutrons) in the nucleus. It is always a whole number.

templates.pattern: An atom has a mass number of [A] and an atomic number of [Z]. Calculate the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
templates.explanation:
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number
= A − Z
= [A] − [Z]
= [RESULT]

Isotopes of the same element have the same atomic number but different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers.

templates.pattern: An atom has a mass number of [A] and [N] neutrons. Calculate the atomic number of the element.
templates.explanation:
Atomic number = mass number − number of neutrons
= A − N
= [A] − [N]
= [RESULT]

The atomic number defines which element an atom is. It equals the number of protons and also the number of electrons in a neutral atom.

templates.pattern: A radioactive source has an initial activity of [A0] Bq. Calculate the activity of the source after one half life in Bq.
templates.explanation:
After one half life the activity halves:
Activity = A₀ ÷ 2
= [A0] ÷ 2
= [RESULT] Bq

The half life is the time taken for the activity of a radioactive source to fall to half its original value. Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq).

templates.pattern: A radioactive source has an initial activity of [A0] Bq. Calculate the activity of the source after two half lives in Bq.
templates.explanation:
After two half lives the activity falls to one quarter:
Activity = A₀ ÷ 4
= [A0] ÷ 4
= [RESULT] Bq

After each half life the activity halves again. After n half lives the activity = A₀ × (0.5)ⁿ.

templates.pattern: A radioactive source has an initial activity of [A0] Bq. Calculate the activity of the source after three half lives in Bq.
templates.explanation:
After three half lives the activity falls to one eighth:
Activity = A₀ ÷ 8
= [A0] ÷ 8
= [RESULT] Bq

The pattern is: after 1 half life → ½, after 2 → ¼, after 3 → ⅛, after 4 → 1/16 and so on.

templates.pattern: A radioactive sample undergoes [N] half lives. Calculate the fraction of the original activity remaining.
templates.explanation:
Fraction remaining = (0.5)ⁿ
= (0.5)^[N]
= [RESULT]

After [N] half lives only [RESULT] of the original activity remains. This exponential decay means a radioactive source never completely disappears — it just gets smaller and smaller.

templates.pattern: A radioactive sample contains [N0] atoms initially. After [N] half lives calculate the number of atoms remaining.
templates.explanation:
Number of atoms remaining = N₀ × (0.5)ⁿ
= [N0] × (0.5)^[N]
= [RESULT]

As atoms decay they transform into different elements. The number of radioactive atoms decreases exponentially with time.

templates.pattern: A radioactive source has a half life of [THALF] years. A sample currently has an activity of [A] Bq. The original activity was [A2] Bq. Calculate the number of half lives that have elapsed.
templates.explanation:
Number of half lives = log₂(A₀ ÷ A)
= log₂([A2] ÷ [A])
= [RESULT]

Each time the activity halves one more half life has elapsed. Count how many times [A2] must be halved to reach [A].

templates.pattern: A radioactive sample has an initial mass of [M0] g. Calculate the mass remaining after [N] half lives in grams.
templates.explanation:
Mass remaining = M₀ × (0.5)ⁿ
= [M0] × (0.5)^[N]
= [RESULT] g

The mass of a radioactive isotope decreases with each half life as atoms decay into different elements. The total mass of all products remains conserved.
